article.headline: The Millionaire List That Forgets Its Casualties
article.lede: Every bull market produces its retrospective roster of life-changing winners. What it does not produce — not willingly, anyway — is the much longer list of names that promised the same journey and delivered something else entirely.
article.body:
The post from @futurist_lens follows a well-worn format: three undeniable victories are stacked in ascending order of cultural resonance — *NVDA*, *TSLA*, *PLTR* — and then a new cohort of candidates is offered as their rightful heirs. The construction is clean and the logic feels intuitive. NVIDIA went public in 1999 at twelve dollars a share; a thousand dollars invested then would, after six stock splits and twenty-six years of patience, be worth well over half a million today. Tesla's 2010 IPO at seventeen dollars produced a return of roughly twenty-two thousand percent for those who held through the years of production hell and Twitter storms. Palantir, which went public by direct listing in 2020, has accelerated sharply, with quarterly revenue growth hitting eighty-five percent year-over-year in early 2026. The victories are real. The framing around them is the problem.

What the format exploits is *survivorship bias* — the cognitive habit of drawing lessons exclusively from the entities that made it through a selection process, while the far larger population of those that did not simply ceases to exist in the rearview. A database study covering twenty-nine thousand US-listed stocks over ninety-eight years found that more than half produced negative cumulative returns over their entire trading lives, with a median compound return of negative seven percent. Every retrospective list of stock-market millionaires is an exercise in selecting the survivors and presenting them as evidence that the game is predictable. The companies that were, in their day, equally compelling stories — with equally urgent social-media threads — are simply gone.

The space-economy cohort the post gestures toward is genuinely interesting on its merits, which makes it worth examining with some care. Rocket Lab (*RKLB*) reported 2025 revenue of six hundred and two million dollars, up thirty-eight percent, with a backlog of 1.85 billion dollars and a reusable medium-lift rocket on track to debut later this year. AST SpaceMobile (*ASTS*), which is building a network of satellites designed to deliver broadband directly to standard mobile phones, generated seventy million dollars in 2025 revenue and has guided for up to two hundred million in 2026. Intuitive Machines (*LUNR*), which lands spacecraft on the Moon under NASA's Artemis program, guided for nine hundred million to one billion dollars in 2026 revenue — nearly five times its trailing figure. These are not vaporous promises; they are companies with contracts, launch records, and hardware in orbit.

But for every RKLB there is a Virgin Orbit, which took the SPAC route to public markets, burned through its capital base, and filed for Chapter Eleven bankruptcy in April 2023 after a high-profile launch failure. Redwire (*RDW*), a manufacturer of spacecraft components that also went public via *SPAC* (a *special-purpose acquisition company*, a blank-check vehicle that merged with an operating business to list it without a traditional IPO), is down roughly twenty-two percent over the past year even as the broader space sector rallied. By 2023, more companies that had gone public through SPACs between 2020 and 2022 were trading below one dollar per share than above ten. The space SPAC class of 2020-2021 is, as a cohort, one of the more instructive recent examples of survivorship bias in formation: the names that made it are now used to argue that the next cohort will also make it, while the names that didn't are quietly unavailable for comment.

The pattern itself is worth naming: *speculative-theme rotation*, the recurring social-media cycle in which a sector is identified as the locus of the next generation of life-altering returns, a handful of publicly traded names are assembled as proxies for the thesis, and the argument is packaged in a format optimized for virality. The format typically features a proven past winner (or three), a credible structural narrative, and a call to action calibrated just short of explicit financial advice. It recurs because the underlying human appetite for a legible path from ordinary means to extraordinary wealth is essentially inexhaustible, and because the format is genuinely difficult to falsify in advance: you cannot know, in May 2026, which of the space-economy names will look, in 2036, like NVDA from the perspective of 2024.

The honest version of the thesis would go something like this: the commercial space economy is a real and expanding industry, several publicly traded companies in it have legitimate revenue growth and defensible competitive positions, and some of them may produce extraordinary returns over a decade. It would also note that many will not, that the ones that do will require either extraordinary foresight or extraordinary patience (or both), and that the act of buying something because a tweet placed it on the same list as NVIDIA is not a strategy. The millionaire-list format is not designed to deliver that version. It is designed to be shared.

concepts.definition: The cognitive error of drawing conclusions only from the entities that survived a selection process — winners, listed companies, successful funds — while ignoring the larger, invisible population that failed. In investing, it makes past returns look more achievable and predictable than they actually were.

A blank-check shell company that raises money through an IPO with the sole purpose of merging with a private operating business, thereby taking it public without the scrutiny of a traditional IPO. Popular with space-economy companies during the 2020-2021 boom; the cohort as a whole subsequently performed poorly.

The recurring social-media cycle in which a macro narrative (AI, space, biotech, crypto) is packaged with a short list of stock-market proxies and circulated as the site of the next generation of outsized returns, typically just after a prior theme has already produced its visible winners.

A method of going public in which existing shareholders sell shares directly on an exchange without the company issuing new shares or hiring underwriters, as Palantir did in September 2020. Avoids underwriter fees but also forgoes the price stabilization of a traditional IPO.

article.fact_check: NVIDIA's 1999 IPO price and subsequent split-adjusted returns are well-documented; the $1,000-to-$560,000 figure refers to a twenty-year window (2006-2026) per U.S. News & World Report. Tesla's 2010 IPO price of $17 and the approximately 22,000% total return figure are per Motley Fool and Pocket Option historical analyses. Palantir's 85% year-over-year revenue growth in Q1 2026 is per Motley Fool's May 2026 earnings report coverage. RKLB's 2025 revenue ($602M, +38%) and backlog ($1.85B) are per 24/7 Wall St. and MarketBeat as of May 2026. ASTS's $70.9M 2025 revenue and 2026 guidance of $150M-$200M are per the same sources. LUNR's 2026 revenue guidance of $900M-$1B is per MarketBeat and 24/7 Wall St., April 2026. Virgin Orbit's April 2023 Chapter 11 filing is publicly documented. The finding that more 2020-2022 SPAC-listed companies traded below $1 than above $10 by April 2023 is per Skadden's quarterly insights report. The 29,000-stock / 98-year study with median return of -7.41% is per Benzinga/Yahoo Finance citing academic research on US equity survivorship bias.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_tsla.name: Tesla Inc.
ticker_tsla.blurb: Tesla designs and manufactures battery-electric vehicles, energy storage systems, and solar products. Founded in 2003 and taken public in June 2010 at seventeen dollars per share, it became one of the most spectacular long-term equity stories of the 2010s: every share from the IPO, adjusted for subsequent stock splits, would be worth roughly 6,500 dollars by late 2025 — a return of approximately 22,000 percent. The company's Model S (2012), Model 3 (2017), and Model Y (2020) progressively expanded the addressable market from luxury to mass-market segments. Tesla also operates a global Supercharger network and a large-scale energy storage division (Megapack). CEO Elon Musk's public profile — across social media, SpaceX, and his acquisition of X (formerly Twitter) — has made Tesla one of the more volatile large-cap equities in recent years, as investor sentiment toward the company has become partially indexed to sentiment toward Musk personally.
ticker_tsla.recent: Tesla has faced intensifying competition from Chinese electric-vehicle manufacturers, particularly BYD, which overtook Tesla in global EV sales in 2023. Revenue growth decelerated sharply in 2024, and the company has relied on price cuts to defend market share, compressing margins. Musk's political visibility during the 2024 US election cycle and his role in the DOGE cost-cutting initiative generated significant consumer backlash in some markets, with Tesla registrations declining in Europe and California in early 2025. The stock traded in a wide range through 2025-2026 as investors weighed the autonomous-vehicle (Full Self-Driving) optionality against near-term margin pressure.

ticker_pltr.name: Palantir Technologies Inc.
ticker_pltr.blurb: Palantir Technologies, founded in 2003 by Peter Thiel, Alex Karp, and others, builds large-scale data-analytics and AI platforms for government intelligence agencies and commercial enterprises. Its flagship products are Gotham (for government and defence clients), Foundry (for commercial enterprises), and the Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP), launched in 2023, which allows organisations to deploy large language models within their existing data infrastructure. The company is headquartered in Denver, Colorado, and is unusual among technology companies in that it derives a substantial share of revenue from classified US government contracts — a relatively insulated revenue stream that also limits disclosure. Palantir built a large retail-investor following due to its association with AI, US defence spending growth, and the outspoken, unconventional public persona of CEO Alex Karp.
ticker_pltr.recent: Palantir's shares reached an all-time high of approximately $207.52 in November 2025, having risen more than 300% from January 2025 on a combination of AI-platform enthusiasm and accelerating commercial revenue growth. The stock suffered a drawdown of roughly 22–38% from that peak through April 2026 — the range reflecting how rapidly sentiment shifted during the broad mega-cap sell-off. As of early May 2026, shares had retraced to around $136, representing a drawdown of more than 34% from the November high.

ticker_rklb.blurb: Rocket Lab Corporation is a Long Beach, California-based vertically integrated space and defense company. It operates two primary business lines: Launch Services (Electron small-sat rocket, HASTE hypersonic test vehicle) and Space Systems (satellite design and manufacture, spacecraft components including solar panels, reaction wheels, star trackers, and radios). Electron, the world's most frequently launched privately-developed small rocket, completed 21 missions in 2025 with a 100% success rate. The company is developing Neutron, a partially reusable medium-lift rocket targeted for first launch in Q4 2026 or early 2027.
ticker_rklb.recent: Full-year 2025 revenue was $602 million (+38% YoY) on a record $1.85 billion backlog (+73% YoY), with a $198 million net loss; Q1 2026 guidance calls for $185–200 million revenue (+57% YoY). In December 2025 Rocket Lab won an $816 million SDA contract to build 18 satellites for the Tracking Layer Tranche 3 missile-warning constellation — its largest ever single contract — and the HASTE hypersonic test program now carries a $190 million block-buy for 20 suborbital flights under MACH-TB 2.0. Neutron development continues at NASA Stennis after a Stage 1 tank rupture during qualification was traced to a manufacturing defect; cumulative program spend is approximately $360 million through end-2025. The stock closed near $78 in early May 2026 against a 52-week range of $20.23–$99.58.

ticker_asts.name: AST SpaceMobile, Inc.
ticker_asts.blurb: AST SpaceMobile is building a network of large-aperture satellites in low Earth orbit designed to deliver broadband directly to unmodified standard mobile handsets — no specialised hardware required. The company has carrier partnerships representing roughly three billion potential subscribers, including AT&T, Verizon, Vodafone, and Rakuten, and secured $1 billion in hard commercial commitments from those partners.
ticker_asts.recent: BlueBird 6, described as the largest commercial communications array ever deployed in LEO, launched aboard an ISRO LVM3 rocket in December 2025. The company targets intermittent US nationwide service in early 2026 and continuous service by late 2026, with 45-60 satellites on orbit by year-end. A 10-year commercial agreement with stc Group (Saudi Arabia) was signed in October 2025.

ticker_lunr.name: Intuitive Machines, Inc.
ticker_lunr.blurb: Intuitive Machines is a space infrastructure and services company that provides payload delivery, data transmission, and lunar surface access services. It offers transportation and delivery of satellites, scientific instruments, and cargo to various destinations in space, as well as data collection, processing, and interpretation using AI applications. The company is a key player in the emerging lunar economy and competes in the aerospace and defense sector.
